rounds.proof_sketch: shared[257] vs shared[256] — all accesses use tid ∈ [0,255] and tid+stride ∈ [0,255]. Index 256 is never read or written. The extra element is dead memory.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation only increases the shared memory allocation from 256 to 257 elements. Since the kernel launches 256 threads per block (blockDim.x=256), the thread index tid ranges [0,255]. All shared memory accesses use indices tid (max 255) or tid+stride (max 255 when stride=128, tid=127). The element at index 256 is never accessed. The computation, reduction logic, and final atomicAdd are all identical. Any observed divergence is due to inherent non-determinism in atomicAdd ordering across blocks, not the mutation.
rounds.kill_strategy: Unkillable — the mutation adds one unused element to shared memory. No input values can cause different code paths or calculations since index 256 is never accessed.
rounds.recommendations: Mutation testing frameworks should recognize array size changes that don't affect actual access bounds as likely equivalent. Static analysis could detect that the additional array element is never referenced.
